title: Into the market with open hands
hookLine: tenth picture: he walks into town with open hands, bringing gifts

lines: A GOURD, A STAFF, OPEN HANDS.
cards: The last picture is noisy. After a silent circle and a quiet river, the herdsman is back, walking into town. Barefoot, chest bare, smeared with dust and ash, a broad grin, and in some drawings a big belly too.
He carries a gourd and a staff, and in some versions a sack over his shoulder. He's headed for the market, the wineshop, the crowd. No robe, no halo, nothing to mark him as special.
Just a cheerful man among people, with his hands open.

teach.h: IT ENDS IN THE MARKET, NOT A CAVE.
teach.b: First, it ends in the market, not a cave. The series could have stopped at the empty circle or the peaceful river.

The Chinese title says he enters the town with hands hanging down, an image of open, relaxed hands, ready to help. In this teaching, awakening that stays on the mountain isn't finished. It comes back down.

teach.h: NOBODY CAN TELL HE'S A SAGE.
teach.b: Second, nobody can tell. The preface, in paraphrase, says his gate is shut and even the wise don't know him; his inner life can't be glimpsed.
He doesn't seek out the footprints of the old masters or try to look like a sage. He goes to market with his gourd and comes home with his staff. Third, what he brings.
The preface says he keeps company with drinkers and butchers, and they all become buddhas.
The verse says he needs no secret art of the immortals, yet in front of him withered trees come into bloom. He doesn't preach or recruit. He's simply among people, and things around him come alive.
Fourth, awakening as ordinary company. In some paintings he looks like Budai, the laughing monk of Chinese folk tradition with his sack of gifts.

Mahayana teaching holds up the bodhisattva, who seeks awakening for the sake of others, and this picture shows that help as ordinary company: buying vegetables, sharing a drink, listening to a neighbor.
The whole search comes out here, at a market stall, with open hands.

how: The oxherding series ends with the tenth picture, which some Zen teachers use to stress that practice returns to daily life and service; in Zen communities this shows up as work practice, care for others and ordinary kindness.

o: leaving town for a quiet mountain cave to meditate
returning to ordinary life with open hands, ready to help
showing off in town so crowds will honor him as a sage

games.q: into the market: tap the pairs.
p: the laughing monk with a sack of gifts
a river; the tenth, a market

s: the oxherding series ends with the herdsman alone on a mountain
it ends in the town marketplace, among people.
the verse says he needs no secret art of the immortals
and yet withered trees come into bloom in front of him.
in the tenth picture he dresses to look like a sage
barefoot, bare-chested, smeared with dust: nothing marks him as special.

games.q: you've been through all nine pictures: searching, catching, the circle, the river. where does the tenth picture send you?
o: deeper into the mountains, away from noise.
into town, to the market, with open hands.
back to the beginning, to search again.
games.why: the series ends in the marketplace. in this teaching, awakening that stays on the mountain isn't finished; it comes back to help.

practice: Let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up and relaxed, the way the herdsman walks into town.

Bring to mind one person you'll likely meet today, at the store, the office or the kitchen, and without making a plan, let one small way of helping them come to mind: a door held, a question asked, five minutes of real listening.

wordCard.voice: Into the market. The tenth oxherding picture: the herdsman returns to town with open hands, ordinary and unnoticed, and the people around him come alive. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (ruchan chuishou): 'entering the market with hands hanging down', the name of the tenth oxherding picture.

carryVoice: Your line: awakening comes back to help. Ten pictures, and the last one is a crowd, met with open hands. See you tomorrow.
